steps.say: Double vision is binocular when one eye closed removes it, and monocular when it persists with one eye shut. Binocular diplopia means the eyes are misaligned from nerve, muscle or junction disease. Monocular diplopia stays in one eye and is optical, from astigmatism with cataract with dry eye. Covering one eye is the first bedside move and it splits the whole topic in seconds.
steps.tx: **Binocular diplopia** vanishes when one eye closes and means **misalignment** from nerve, muscle or junction disease. **Monocular diplopia** persists with one eye shut and is **optical** (astigmatism, cataract, dry eye). **Cover testing** splits the topic in seconds. New binocular diplopia with headache or pupil change is **never routine**.

steps.say: A complete third nerve palsy drops the lid with a down and out eye that cannot look in or up. When the pupil is blown, a posterior communicating artery aneurysm is compressing the nerve and it may bleed at any moment. Pupil sparing in a vasculopath points to ischaemia that recovers alone. Scanning is immediate for every pupil involved palsy, while ischaemic ones are watched with vascular control.
steps.tx: **Third nerve palsy** gives ptosis with a **down and out** eye that cannot adduct or elevate. A **blown pupil** means **posterior communicating aneurysm** compression and possible rupture. **Pupil sparing** in vasculopaths means **ischaemia** that recovers alone. Every pupil involved palsy gets an **urgent angiogram**.

steps.say: A fourth nerve palsy tilts the head away from the weak side to fuse the images, and the patient complains of vertical double vision on stairs. Trauma is the commonest acquired cause, followed by ischaemia in vasculopaths. The Bielschowsky head tilt test confirms it, with worsening on looking down and in. Most ischaemic cases resolve, while traumatic ones may need prism or muscle surgery.
steps.tx: **Fourth nerve palsy** tilts the head **away** from the lesion to fuse vertical images. **Trauma** is the commonest acquired cause, then vasculopathic ischaemia. **Bielschowsky head tilt** confirms it: worse looking down and in. **Ischaemic** cases resolve in months; traumatic ones may need **prism or surgery**.

steps.say: A sixth nerve palsy cannot abduct the eye, so the face turns toward the weak side to keep single vision. It is the great false localiser, because raised pressure stretches it far from the actual lesion. Lumbar puncture opening pressure with M R I venography follows when both sides fail together. Isolated vasculopathic cases recover, but bilateral disease is scanned and tapped without delay.
steps.tx: **Sixth nerve palsy** cannot **abduct**; the face turns toward the lesion. It is the classic **false localiser** of raised intracranial pressure. **Bilateral** sixth palsies need **MRI plus venography** and pressure measurement. **Isolated vasculopathic** cases recover in months with risk control.

steps.say: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia breaks adduction on one side with nystagmus of the other eye, because the medial longitudinal fasciculus is cut. Young adults point to multiple sclerosis, while older vasculopaths point to stroke. One and a half syndrome adds a gaze palsy on the same side, leaving only the far eye moving out. Convergence is spared, which separates it from a third nerve palsy.
steps.tx: **INO** fails **adduction** on one side with **nystagmus** of the abducting eye; the **MLF** is cut. **Young** patients point to **MS**, older vasculopaths to **stroke**. **One and a half syndrome** adds ipsilateral gaze failure. **Convergence spared** separates INO from third nerve disease.

steps.say: Myasthenia gravis fatigues through the day, so lids droop by evening and double vision comes and goes with effort. The ice test lifts a tired lid within minutes, and sustained upgaze tires it again. Antibodies to acetylcholine receptors confirm most generalised cases, while single fibre studies catch the rest. Steroids with signal boosting drugs control most, and thymectomy helps selected young patients.
steps.tx: **Myasthenia** gives **fatigable ptosis and diplopia**, worse by evening. The **ice test** lifts the lid within minutes. **Acetylcholine receptor antibodies** confirm most; single fibre EMG catches the rest. **Signal boosting drugs** with **steroids** control most cases. **Thymectomy** helps young generalised disease.

steps.say: Miller Fisher syndrome completes the triad of drooping eyes with unsteady gait with absent reflexes after a diarrhoeal illness. Antibodies to G Q one b confirm it, and spinal fluid shows protein without cells after the first week. Most patients recover fully with immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, and the eyes lead the recovery. It is the cranial variant of Guillain Barre syndrome, not a stroke.
steps.tx: **Miller Fisher** gives **ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia** after gut infection. **GQ1b antibodies** confirm it; CSF shows **protein without cells**. **Immunoglobulin or plasma exchange** speeds recovery, and most recover fully. It is a **Guillain Barre variant**, so stroke thrombolysis must never be given.

steps.say: Thyroid eye disease pushes the eyes forward with a staring lid lag, and it strikes smokers with Graves disease hardest. The inferior with medial recti swell first, so looking up then out fails early. Optic nerve compression at the apex blinds silently, and it is tested with colour with fields in every case. Selenium helps mild disease, while steroids with decompression rescue sight threatening cases.
steps.tx: **Thyroid eye disease** gives **proptosis with lid lag** in Graves smokers. **Inferior then medial recti** fail first, so upgaze then side gaze is lost. **Apical compression** blinds silently; colour and fields are tested always. **Selenium** suits mild disease. **Steroids** with **orbital decompression** rescue sight threatening cases.

steps.say: Every new double vision follows the same bedside order before any scan. Cover testing splits optical from misalignment, then lids with pupils with movements name the nerve. Fatigability with ice testing hunts myasthenia, while headache with pupil change triggers angiography. Only then does imaging follow the named suspect, which keeps scans few and diagnoses fast.
steps.tx: **Bedside order** is fixed: **cover test** first, then lids, pupils and movements. **Fatigue and ice** hunt myasthenia. **Headache or blown pupil** triggers **angiography**. **MRI brain** follows the named nerve; bilateral sixths add **venography**. Scanning before examining wastes the test and misses the named nerve.

steps.say: Aneurysmal third nerve palsy is coiled or clipped within hours, and delay blinds or kills. Ischaemic palsies recover with control of sugar with pressure with lipids, needing no surgery. Myasthenia is managed with signal boosting drugs with steroids with thymectomy selection. Thyroid compression is decompressed, and Miller Fisher receives immunotherapy. Prism glasses with patching bridge every recovery.
steps.tx: **Aneurysm** compression is **coiled or clipped** within hours. **Ischaemic** palsies recover with vascular control alone. **Myasthenia** takes signal drugs with steroids; thymectomy is selected. **Thyroid apex** compression is decompressed. **Prisms and patching** bridge recovery in all groups while diplopia persists.

steps.say: For the exam, the facts to lock in are cover testing first, blown pupil means aneurysm, pupil sparing means ischaemia, head tilt away for fourth nerve, false localiser for sixth nerve, adduction failure for I N O, and fatigable lids with ice test for myasthenia. Miller Fisher is indicated by G Q one b while thyroid stare indicates Graves. Memorise the facts in this table exactly as written.
steps.tx: **High yield for the exam:** **cover testing** splits diplopia first. **Blown pupil** means aneurysm; spared pupil means ischaemia. **Fourth nerve** tilts away; **sixth nerve** is the false localiser. **INO** fails adduction. **Fatigable lids** with ice test mark myasthenia. **GQ1b** marks Miller Fisher.
